coarse_filters.approx_climate_biome: semi-arid high-altitude Andean valley (dry winter, deciduous/thorny trees)

cues.observation: ENTEL logo (blue oval with swoosh) painted directly on building corners, plus 'aqui entel' A-frame sign — ENTEL is Bolivia's state telecom, painted on walls exactly this way nationwide.
Tigo Money yellow shop sign ('Agresivo Net') and Tigo wall paint — Tigo operates in Bolivia, Paraguay, Guatemala; combined with ENTEL it is decisively Bolivian.
Construction banner for CONCRETEC and FANCESA cement — FANCESA (Fábrica Nacional de Cemento S.A.) is headquartered in Sucre and dominates the Chuquisaca/Potosí market.
Landline numbers beginning '645xxxx' on the cement banner — Bolivian 7-digit format with area code 4 region... the 64/65 prefixes correspond to the Sucre/Chuquisaca-Potosí exchange block.
Blue Nissan Civilian minibus marked line '6' with hand-painted lettering, typical Bolivian urban 'micro' fleet of imported Japanese right-hand-drive-converted minibuses.
Unplastered orange hollow-brick multi-storey houses with exposed rebar and shallow-pitch roofs, stacked on steep slopes — Andean Bolivian self-built urbanism.
Older colonial-era single-storey adobe row houses with whitewash and red clay tile roofs on narrow cobbled/concrete lanes — colonial valley city core rather than an altiplano new town.
Leafy but partly leafless deciduous street trees, dry brown grass, strong dry-season sun with deep shadows — high valley at ~2700-2900 m, warmer/greener than La Paz/El Alto altiplano.
Woman in pleated skirt with shawl and light straw/felt hat — Andean chola dress; the tall stovepipe/white broad hat style fits Chuquisaca/Potosí rather than the bowler hat of La Paz.
Concrete utility poles with simple crossarms, tangled low-voltage drops, yellow-and-black striped bollards, whitewashed kerbs.
Vehicles drive on the right; no lane paint on concrete-slab residential streets; blue market stalls and tarps along a park edge.

narrowing.question: Which continent and hemisphere?

narrowing.discriminator: Central American towns at this density would show Coca-Cola/Claro-dominated tin-roof commerce and lush humid vegetation; African or South Asian scenes would lack Spanish and would use different minibus stock and left-hand traffic in much of Africa/India.
ruled_out: Africa — Spanish signage and Andean architecture absent there
South Asia — no Devanagari/other scripts, right-hand traffic with Spanish text
Central America — high-altitude dry Andean valley vegetation and 4-5 storey brick towers do not match

narrowing.question: Bolivia, Peru, or Ecuador?
narrowing.observation: ENTEL blue-oval logos painted on two different building corners plus Tigo Money branding on a shop awning, and a CONCRETEC/FANCESA cement banner with a .com.bo web address.
narrowing.discriminator: Peru would show Movistar/Claro/Bitel wall paint and Cementos Pacasmayo or Yura branding; Ecuador would show CNT/Claro and Holcim; Argentina would have Personal/Movistar and no ENTEL-Tigo pairing. ENTEL+Tigo+FANCESA is uniquely Bolivian.
ruled_out: Peru — no Movistar/Claro/Bitel paint, wrong cement brands
Ecuador — CNT branding absent, architecture and dress differ
Argentina — no Andean chola dress, different telecom and vehicle mix

narrowing.question: Altiplano/La Paz basin, temperate valleys, or eastern lowlands?
narrowing.observation: Leafy deciduous street trees, jacaranda-like canopy, whitewashed adobe with red tiles, but hilly terrain and thin bright light; no treeless altiplano flatness and no tropical palms or lowland galvanized-roof sprawl.
narrowing.discriminator: El Alto/La Paz would be essentially treeless with brick towers on bare ochre ground and aymara bowler hats; Santa Cruz would be flat, humid, palm-lined, with motorcycle-dominant traffic and no hillside stacking.
ruled_out: La Paz/El Alto — street tree canopy and tiled colonial adobe are absent up there
Santa Cruz — no tropical vegetation, wrong climate and building materials

narrowing.question: Cochabamba, Chuquisaca (Sucre), Potosí, or Tarija?
narrowing.observation: Building-site banner advertises FANCESA cement together with CONCRETEC, and the contact numbers are 7-digit lines starting 645xxxx.
narrowing.discriminator: Cochabamba sites overwhelmingly advertise Cemento COBOCE (a local cooperative) and use 4-4xxxxxx numbers; Tarija uses El Puente/Warnes brands with 4-6xxxxx of a different block; Potosí city would sit above 4000 m with no leafy deciduous canopy and stark treeless slopes. FANCESA is the Sucre-based plant and its banners saturate Chuquisaca.
ruled_out: Cochabamba — COBOCE branding would dominate instead of FANCESA
Tarija — different cement suppliers and a warmer, vineyard-valley streetscape
Potosí city — far too high and cold for this tree canopy

narrowing.question: Historic colonial core or peripheral hillside barrio of Sucre?
narrowing.observation: Mixed fabric: one frame shows a wide avenue with a park, open-air market tarps and a mid-rise tower on the skyline, others show narrow steep lanes of raw brick 4-5 storey self-builds with unfinished facades and dirt spoil heaps.
narrowing.discriminator: Sucre's declared colonial core is uniformly whitewashed with strict two-storey height and tiled roofs and no exposed-brick towers or unpaved shoulders; what we see is the transitional ring around a neighbourhood market, i.e. outside the protected centre.
ruled_out: central historic core (Plaza 25 de Mayo area) — exposed raw-brick multi-storey blocks and unmade ground would not be permitted there
narrowing.conclusion: Peripheral market barrio on the sloping edge of Sucre (e.g. mercado-adjacent neighbourhood a few km from the core)

analysis.cultural_economic_read: A lower-middle-income Andean city neighbourhood: incremental self-built housing (hollow brick, exposed rebar for future floors) financed floor-by-floor, informal street commerce under tarps, phone-credit and mobile-money kiosks (ENTEL, Tigo Money) as the main retail service, and 1990s Japanese-import sedans plus small minibuses providing transport rather than a formal bus system. Quechua-speaking Andean population is indicated by traditional pollera-and-hat dress; the coexistence of whitewashed tile-roofed colonial adobe rows with raw-brick towers marks a colonial valley city under rapid informal densification, with cement supply and construction as visible local economic drivers.

analysis.cultural_economic_read: Lower-middle-income Andean city periphery in a Quechua-speaking inter-Andean valley. The economy visible here is informal-retail plus construction: mobile-money agents (Tigo Money) and ENTEL top-up shops occupying ground floors, a locally branded cement supply chain (FANCESA/CONCRETEC) feeding continuous incremental self-build, and privately operated micro-buses (line 6, Nissan Civilian) rather than a municipal transit authority. Households finance housing floor-by-floor, leaving upper storeys unrendered with protruding rebar. Vehicle stock is 1990s used Japanese imports. Traditional pollera-and-hat dress alongside modern shopfronts indicates a mixed mestizo/Quechua population, and a modern high-rise on the horizon shows capital concentrating in the formal centre while the slopes grow informally.

correction.summary: Sucre, Chuquisaca (Bolivia) confirmed with 0.63 km error. The ENTEL blue-oval wall paintings plus Tigo/Tigo Money agent signage fixed Bolivia against Peru/Argentina/Chile; the FANCESA-CONCRETEC construction banner with a 645xxxx local number plus mature valley shade trees and steep raw-brick incremental hillside blocks fixed Sucre over Cochabamba, Potosí and the altiplano. The district call (unregulated northwestern hillside periphery rather than the whitewashed UNESCO core) was also correct.

discriminators.title: ENTEL blue oval wall paint vs Peru's Movistar/Claro murals
discriminators.body: In Bolivia peri-urban walls carry a hand-painted blue ENTEL oval, often paired with orange 'Tigo Money' agent boards. In Peru you would instead see green Bitel, red Claro or turquoise Movistar wall paint with BCP/Interbank agent stickers, and no Tigo at all. The ENTEL+Tigo pair is effectively a Bolivia lock.

discriminators.title: FANCESA hoardings mark Chuquisaca; COBOCE marks Cochabamba
discriminators.body: Bolivian construction-site banners advertise the regional cement supplier: FANCESA (with CONCRETEC) around Sucre and Chuquisaca. In Cochabamba you would instead see COBOCE branding, and around La Paz/Oruro SOBOCE/Viacha. Reading the cement brand narrows a Bolivian valley city faster than architecture does.

discriminators.title: Valley canopy vs treeless altiplano in Bolivia
discriminators.body: Sucre-type inter-Andean valley streets show mature jacaranda/molle shade trees and grassy strip parks, dry-brown in winter but with real canopy. On the altiplano (El Alto, Oruro, Potosí) you would instead see no broadleaf canopy, only eucalyptus rows or bare ground, plus colder-weather dress and paler flat horizons.

discriminators.title: Raw-brick hillside periphery vs whitewashed UNESCO core
discriminators.body: In Sucre's hillside expansion districts nearly every building is exposed red brick with unrendered top floors, rebar stubs and unpaved lot edges. In the UNESCO 'Ciudad Blanca' core you would instead see uniformly whitewashed façades, red-tile eaves and wooden colonial balconies with no bare brick. A single surviving pantiled row house on a peripheral avenue does not indicate the core.

discriminators.title: Bolivian micro fleet vs Argentine formal city buses
discriminators.body: Bolivian valley cities run small Japanese Civilian/Coaster minibuses in operator liveries with hand-painted route numbers and destination boards. In Argentina you would instead see full-size colectivos with standardised line liveries, electronic destination signs and Mercosur yellow-and-black plates on European-market cars.
